alt: The same whitetail buck relief carved at three sizes, large, medium and small, standing side by side on a workbench
scene: THREE COPIES OF THE SAME CARVING AT THREE SIZES, wide magazine shot. The exact panel from image 1, finished in the house finish, appears three times standing upright side by side on the bench, left to right: a large one about 60 cm wide, a medium one about 40 cm wide, and a small one about 22 cm wide. All three are the identical design, identical finish, identical proportions, only the size differs, like a family of nesting prints. The large one is razor sharp with every hair and leaf readable; the smallest still reads clearly but its finest antler tines and leaf veins are visibly softer. A steel rule lies along the front edge of the bench. Warm window light from the left. Nothing overlaps; all three fully visible.

alt: Two copies of the same relief seen edge-on: one carved at full depth with clear layers, one flattened so the layers collapse
scene: EDGE-ON COMPARISON. Two copies of the panel from image 1, both in the house finish, lie flat on the bench and are photographed from a very low angle almost level with the surface, so their carved profiles read as silhouettes against soft light. The NEAR panel is carved at FULL depth: the buck's head stands up proud, roughly 14 mm above the background, with the antlers, the ears and the forest behind clearly stepped at different heights, like a mountain range in profile. The FAR panel is the same design carved at ONE THIRD the depth: everything is squashed into a shallow ripple, the layers have collapsed together and it looks flat and lifeless from this angle. A small steel depth gauge stands beside the near panel. Raking light from the left exaggerates the difference.

alt: Macro of a carved eye with a tiny tapered ball nose cutter held beside it for scale
scene: EXTREME MACRO on the eye and brow of the carved face from image 1, finished in the house finish, with the tip of a tiny 1/16 inch tapered ball nose cutter held horizontally right beside the eye by a hand entering from the right, so the cutter's ball tip and the eye's finest carved lines can be compared at the same scale: the lash line and the crease of the lid are only a little wider than the ball. Very shallow depth of field, the eye and the cutter tip tack sharp, everything else soft. Raking light from the left.

alt: A small test tile of the buck's head carved on an offcut, held up against the full panel
scene: A hand holds up a small square TEST TILE, about 8 cm square, cut from an offcut of the same cherry, raw pale unfinished wood, fresh from the machine. Carved on the tile is an EXACT CROP of the buck's head from image 1: THE SAME head, THE SAME pose, THE SAME antlers, ears and eye, at the same angle, as if a square had been cut out of the big panel's design around the head and carved on its own. It must be recognisably the identical animal, not a different deer. Behind the tile, slightly out of focus, stands the full finished panel from image 1 in the house finish, so the viewer can compare the head on the tile with the same head on the panel. The tile is tack sharp and fills about a third of the frame. Workshop light from the left.
